subject: English
passage: Ming Shin, Deepa Menon, and colleagues studied how members of a coastal community in the Solomon Islands describe directions while navigating near-shore reefs. The researchers recorded fishers explaining directional terms, such as vaka mai, a motion-oriented phrase that translates to "coming toward us," and coded each speaker's accompanying hand gestures. Previous research has found a tendency in many seafaring cultures to describe directions at sea using body-relative spatial reference (i.e., relative to the orientation of the speaker): for instance, Portuguese-speaking fishers in the Azores typically gesture toward their own left or right when describing the path of a vessel. In a marine anthropology paper, a student claims that body-relative reference during navigation is universal.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the student's claim?

choices.A: A Solomon Islands fisher gestures in opposite directions when indicating an incoming versus an outgoing vessel.
choices.B: Some grammatical structures used by Solomon Islands fishers when discussing navigation are also used by Portuguese-speaking fishers.
choices.C: When Solomon Islands fishers at sea use gestures to refer to an approaching vessel, they point toward the prevailing swell regardless of which way they are facing.
choices.D: Although Solomon Islands fishers and Portuguese fishers both use gestures when describing navigation, Solomon Islands fishers tend to use fewer gestures overall than Portuguese fishers do.

explanation: Choice C is the best answer. The passage explains that body-relative (egocentric) spatial reference means describing direction relative to the orientation of the speaker, as when Portuguese-speaking fishers gesture toward their own left or right. If Solomon Islands fishers point toward the prevailing swell regardless of which way they are facing, their gestures are fixed to an environmental feature rather than to their own body orientation. That is an allocentric system, not a body-relative one, and would show that body-relative reference during navigation is not universal — directly weakening the student's claim.
